extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and research-integrity professionals (readers of Retraction Watch)
extracted.subtask_description: A curated weekend roundup of recent reporting, commentary, and developments about research misconduct, retractions, AI in scholarship, and peer review quality. Links and short summaries point to items of interest for those tracking scientific integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review report length
rubrics_metrics.description: "The best peer review reports are at least 947 words."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement (from a linked item) that high-quality peer review reports tend to be long (>=947 words). Implies report thoroughness correlates with length; used here as an empirical benchmark rather than a formal standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference integrity (no retracted citations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expression of concern because "the reference list included in this article contains a number of articles that have been retracted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors/reviewers should check reference lists for retracted articles; inclusion of retracted works in references can trigger expressions of concern or corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish code to support reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "AlphaFold3 — why did Nature publish it without its code?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied norm that code underlying reported results should be made available; failure to publish code can provoke outcry and questions about reproducibility and editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify AI-generated citations
rubrics_metrics.description: "The GPTs that offer scholarly citations may eliminate the issue of hallucinated (fake) citations, but they pose other problems."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When authors or tools generate citations (e.g., via GPTs), those citations must be checked for accuracy and provenance; AI may reduce some problems but introduces others requiring verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy/handling for AI use in manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal taking "corrective actions" after learning author used ChatGPT to update references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may require disclosure of AI use and may take corrective actions if undisclosed AI-assisted edits (even to references) are discovered; implies need for explicit editorial policies on AI tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentivize post-publication error detection
rubrics_metrics.description: "Pay researchers to spot errors in published papers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy recommendation to provide financial or formal incentives for researchers to identify and report errors in the literature, strengthening post-publication review and correction mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stronger data-integrity safeguards in journals
rubrics_metrics.description: "Data integrity watchdogs call for stronger safeguards in scientific journals."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should adopt more stringent data-integrity checks, screening, and policies to prevent publication of fabricated, falsified, or unreliable data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional rules curbing AI-assisted theses
rubrics_metrics.description: In China, "Universities issue own rules to curb AI-assisted theses."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities may implement local policies limiting or regulating the use of generative AI in student theses and dissertations to preserve academic standards and authorship integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: National/cultural reform for misconduct handling
rubrics_metrics.description: "A national effort is needed to change the culture around addressing research misconduct in the UK, according to a report by the UK Research Integrity Office."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond procedural fixes, systemic and cultural changes at national/institutional levels are recommended to improve detection, reporting, and handling of research misconduct.
